text: Every morning I lay on the floor in the front parlour watching her door, keeping the blind pulled down to within an inch of the sash so that I could not be seen. <break time="0.8s" /> When she came out on the doorstep, my heart leaped, and I ran to the hall, seized my books, and followed her, always keeping her brown figure in my eye. <break time="0.8s" /> I had never spoken to her, except for a few casual words, and yet her name was like a summons to all my foolish blood. <break time="0.8s" /> Her image accompanied me even in places the most hostile to romance, such as the crowded market where my aunt went shopping on Saturday evenings. <break time="0.8s" /> We walked through the flaring streets, jostled by drunken men and bargaining women, amid the curses of labourers and the shrill cries of shop boys. <break time="0.8s" /> These noises converged in a single sensation of life for me, and I imagined that I bore my chalice safely through a throng of foes. <break time="0.8s" /> One evening I went into the back drawing room in which the priest had died, and it was a dark, rainy evening, and there was no sound in the house. <break time="0.8s" /> Pressing the palms of my hands together until they trembled, I murmured, O love, O love, many times.
